work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In dictum apostoli: Non quod volo facio

paragraphs.text: I praise your longing, I marvel at your zeal, and I welcome this noble rivalry. For this is not a disturbance that breeds uproar, but an affliction that weaves a crown of righteousness. I call blessed your fine eagerness, for whose sake you endure every hardship, clinging to the divine citadel. But just as I marvel at this zeal, so I turn away from labor spent on vain things. Yesterday this sacred assembly of ours was plundered, and instead of this divine and blessed stadium, the hippodrome received the people. And I marveled that you went looking for a contest of horses and abandoned the contest of the divine word. There one could see a race of horses, but here the chariot of God, ten-thousandfold, in which are thousands who steer it. There one could see contest and racing and strife; here, longing and zeal and eagerness. One chariot overthrows ten thousand chariots. For the chariot of God is one, but the chariots of the wicked are many. The one keeps the course of piety straight; the others are overturned by the divine chariot. For, it says, "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God. They were tripped up and fell, but we have risen and stand upright." This chariot does not throw down horses or overturn men. It scatters demons and lays the devil's tyranny flat on the ground. God has a chariot not drawn by four horses but assembled from countless souls. For, it says, "The chariot of God is ten-thousandfold, in which are thousands who steer it." God's horses are the holy souls; God's horses are the souls of the apostles, which traveled through all the earth bringing salvation to the world. For the riding of the apostles is the salvation of the inhabited world. That is why the prophet proclaimed beforehand, saying, "You mounted your horses upon the sea, and your riding is salvation." For these same horses brought salvation to the faithful and troubled the enemies of piety. "You mounted your horses upon the sea," it says, "stirring up many waters." The preaching of the apostles stirred up the gatherings of the nations. Many kings were troubled; many tyrants were thrown into confusion, unable to bear the course of apostolic grace. That is why those who were troubled at the apostles' course said, "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too." See the chariot of God; see horses accepting the bridle of piety. Do not resist the word of truth, and do not imitate the bucking of brute beasts by kicking away the divine law, lest the divine Word say to you as well, "Why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads." Let us accept the bridle of piety and turn our eyes to a chaste spectacle. Let us look at the charioteers of piety, the prophets and apostles. The prophets are charioteers of truth, steering the course of good order. Such was Elijah, to whom Elisha cried out, "Father, father, charioteer of Israel and its horseman!" Piety must be honored above all things. Do not cling to the teaching when you are listening to the divine word, and then, once you are away from the word, show yourself among creatures without reason. Let your soul and your eye be of one mind, and love the word of God. Do not divide your gaze between a shameful spectacle and godly zeal. Train your eye to look at nothing but the beauties of heaven, so that you may say, "To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven." Train your hearing not to listen to shouting or uproar but to the divine law, saying, "I will incline my ear to a parable, and I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me." One must not say what leads to flattery, but teach what disciplines. For there is no gain in flattery, but great profit in discipline. Do not let your mind be taken captive by unseemly spectacles, and do not surrender your thoughts to the songs outside. For reason is able to prevail [?], even if habit is drawing your mind away. You are not a slave but free. You are not taken captive against your will; you willingly sell yourself to sin. Do not seize on the apostle's words. When the reproof of truth comes in and exposes the secrets of the heart, do not say, "Am I better than Paul, who says, 'What I want, I do not do, but what I hate, that I do'?" Do not let habit enslave you into slandering the divine words. Do not, while gratifying your own desire, malign the apostle's glory. For many often make excuses for their sins and hold up to us the apostolic passage that was just read to us. "Paul," they say, "the chosen vessel, who was guided at all times by the Holy Spirit, said: 'What I want, I do not do, but what I hate, that I do. I delight in the law of God in my inner self, but I see another law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin.'" Every lover of sin likes to find some credible figure to fight on the side of his sin, and such people gladly run down the apostles, not to insult them but to provide a defense for themselves. "Paul said," one says, "'For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh.' If then nothing good dwells in Paul, how can good dwell in me? How can I share in the good, and how can the root of good be in me? If we find so great a man taken captive by sin, as he himself made plain, what hope is there for me, wretched as I am and enslaved to sin?" So, lest two evils result—that the apostle's word is slandered, and that we procure for ourselves license to sin—it is necessary to unfold the apostle's whole meaning. The key to everything disputed in the Scriptures is the subject at hand. For when someone knows the speaker's aim, and to whom the words are addressed, and about whom, he gives a clear and unconfused interpretation of the words.

To put it clearly and concisely, the apostle paints a portrait of the whole human being: the one formed in the beginning, the one schooled under the law, and the one set free by grace. He paints it in words, as in a picture. What, then, was Adam before the commandment? And what did he become after the commandment? What condition did he have under the law, and what name did he receive under grace? Suppose I were to say today, "God made us in his image and likeness, but since we transgressed the commandment we were cast out of paradise." I would not be taking those words as being about me personally; rather, I would be applying the ancient history to myself. For I never saw paradise, nor was I cast out of paradise; but I depict what our father suffered and the origin of the calamity, and I say, "I was formed, I transgressed, I was cast out, I was schooled, I was called back." In the same way Paul describes what Adam was before the commandment of the law—I mean the law given in paradise—and says in the person of Adam, "I was once alive apart from the law." Was Paul older than the law? Paul flourished after all who were brought up under the law, after the appearing of Christ. If, then, he comes after the law, how can he present himself as older than the law? Yet his words show that he was older than the law: "I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came to life." Did the commandment come after Paul? And lest anyone suppose that the law existed before Paul, but that he himself once lived apart from the law, having taken up a pagan way of life, and was afterward schooled by the law, the historical record establishes the truth. For there was never a time when Paul lived without the law. He who says, "a Hebrew of Hebrews, circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel"—when did he ever live without the law? "I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came." Which commandment? The one that says, "From every tree in paradise you shall eat." "But when the commandment came, sin came to life, and I died." See how in his words he sets sin and righteousness on a scale: sin is put to death when the commandment is kept, and man dies when sin prospers. For the saying "when the commandment came, sin came to life" shows that sin was dead before the transgression. By "sin" he means not the act of sinning but the devil. Why does he call the devil "sin"? Because he became the teacher of sin. For anyone who does not pay attention to the idioms of Scripture slips badly and misses the mark of the truth. It is Scripture's custom to call the devil "sin." Why? Because he became the teacher, introducer and promoter of sin. Likewise Scripture calls our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, "righteousness," not as an act of righteousness but as the teacher of righteousness. That is why Paul says of him, "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." Just as Christ has been called righteousness because he is the fountain of righteousness, so the devil, having become the introducer and teacher of sin, received the name "sin." "Sin came to life, and I died; and the commandment that was meant for life turned out to bring me death." For God gave Adam a commandment not so that he might die but so that he might live. So the commandment, he says, which was given to me for life, turned out to bring death—not because it was changed, but because through my transgression I overturned its life-giving power. We must attend carefully to every question that arises. For the enemy of the Scriptures, who has not been nourished on the word of piety, immediately resorts to nothing but this: "Did God not foreknow," he says, "that Adam was going to sin? Did he not foreknow that he would not keep the commandment? Did he not foreknow that he would be deceived by the serpent? Why, then, did he give the commandment to one who was not going to keep it?" But we must understand that God foreknows all things, yet gives his laws with an eye not only to the one who transgresses but also to the one who will do right. Why do you say, "Did God not foreknow that Adam would sin?" Why do you pass over in silence what follows and what comes as its consequence? You keep silent out of ill will. But I proclaim in faith that just as God foreknew that Adam would transgress, so he knew that Abel would be justified; he foreknew that Enoch would be translated; he foreknew that the choir of the saints would be formed; he foreknew that Noah would swim through the universal destruction; he foreknew that Abraham, the root of faith, would blossom; he foreknew that patriarchs would shine, prophets would flourish, and apostles would be distinguished; and that from the very lump that was going to transgress would blossom the much-hymned beauty of the Savior's dispensation. He foresaw the course of the apostles; he foresaw the steadfastness of the martyrs; he foresaw the struggles of the confessors; he foresaw the communities of monks; he foresaw the flowering of the churches; he foresaw the choir of priests; he foresaw all who stand in truth at the altar. What then? Was it not right, foreknowing so many good things, to bring his creature into being? "For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me." "Sin"—that is, the devil. "Seizing an opportunity." What opportunity? God had said, "From every tree in paradise you may freely eat, but from the tree of knowing good and evil you shall not eat; for on the day you eat of it you shall surely die." The devil, seizing an opportunity from the commandment, fabricates a slander and says to him, "For God knew that on the day you eat, you will become like gods, and he forbade you." He slanders God as envious and runs him down as begrudging. "God begrudges you equality with God," he says, "and so he forbade you to eat from the tree from which godlike status was going to spring up for you." "So sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me." He was right to say "deceived." For he promised the truth, yet he deceived, "and through it killed me." For the deception gave birth to death. The creature was not mortal. Many have supposed this as well, that God made the creature mortal. But the creature was not mortal. Though it was made of earth, it was fashioned immortal. If it was not created immortal but mortal, why did it receive by sentence what it already had by nature? If this creature was mortal, why does God set death as the penalty for its transgression? "For on the day you eat, you shall surely die." Therefore, before he ate, the creature was immortal. But if it was mortal even before he ate, then what was said is deceit and mockery, not truth, for he threatens me with what I already was. No one threatens someone with sleep, which he has by nature. No one threatens someone with food, which he takes by nature. But God threatens death. What the creature did not have from its creation, it received through sin. For if Adam had remained in the commandment and kept the divine law, death would have had no place. And that wise saying bears witness that "God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living; but through the devil's envy death entered the world." Hence, if we are to speak truly, mortality came upon us contrary to nature, while the resurrection restores to us what accords with nature. That is why it is called a resurrection, a standing up again: because the creature that was corrupted and fell through sin is set upright through righteousness. If Adam had remained in the commandment, he would have remained alive. And who guarantees this statement, so that it may not be thought mere conjecture and plausibility? So then, brothers, that we may not approach divine things with conjectures, but may follow the sequence of events and grasp the clear truth of the matter: what came afterward bears witness to the creature's immortality. If the creature was mortal by nature, if it received death not through sin but through its very nature, how did Elijah and Enoch overcome nature? How was Elijah taken up without tasting death? How was Enoch translated without experiencing death? See the pledges of the original creation: man could have lived forever, had he lived in accordance with the divine law. That is why God took firstfruits of our race and carried them over into immortality. And see the wisdom of his dispensation. He takes up Enoch many generations earlier; he snatches up Elijah many generations later—and this to good purpose. For since piety was to be practiced among two peoples, the people that had uncircumcision and the people that professed circumcision, he does not take up Elijah alone, lest the Jew should boast and pride himself on the firstfruits. Instead he first takes Enoch, who did not live by the law but kept the good order of the church. For everything before the law was a type of the church. Ask who the righteous were up to Abraham and the law. Everything turns on three names: Hellenism, the portion of unbelief; Judaism, which lived according to the law; and Christianity, which is guided by the grace of the gospel. Let our opponents be asked about Adam, Abel, Enoch, Seth, Noah and all who were distinguished from his time until Abraham: who were they? Greeks? But faith does not allow it. They were not Greeks. For they did not live in unbelief, did not serve demons, did not submit to carved idols; they resisted the error of the demons. So they cannot be called Greeks. What, then, were they? Jews? But they did not receive the law; they did not keep sabbaths; they did not observe distinctions of food; they did not have circumcision. If, then, the ancients were neither Greeks nor Jews, another name has been found that can fit them. If indeed those who lived before the law were neither Jews nor Greeks, what title will they give them? What is left? Clearly, Christians—not in name, but in power. That is why all the types of the church shone out beforehand. Enoch was uncircumcised, as is the church. He is not enslaved to the law, just like the people of Christ. He knows no distinctions of food, just like the church that lives by the divine word. The church, ordered according to the pattern of piety, is older than all. And Abraham's faith was an image not of the Jews but of the church. That is why the apostle examines the question of faith closely, and, wishing to show that Abraham is an image of the church and not of the Jews, he says, "Brothers, it is written that Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. When, then, was it credited to him? When he was circumcised, or when he was uncircumcised?" This is Paul speaking, the man from among the Jews, who knew the law and explains the things of the law: "Not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised; and he received circumcision as a sign, a seal of the righteousness he had while uncircumcised." See the contemplation of intricate thoughts. See how the apostle moves Israel out of Abraham's household, since it lacks kinship in faith, and moves the Gentiles in, since they bear the stamp of piety. "And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of righteousness, so that he might become the father of all who believe while uncircumcised." Do you see how the type of the church was lived out in Abraham? And the Savior too wished to show that the order of the gospel leads back to the ancient order. When the Jews said, "Moses wrote: If anyone wishes to divorce his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce," the Savior in turn, setting beside it [?] what was in the law—not to undo it, but to reveal the true teaching—says, "Moses said this because of your hardness of heart; but from the beginning it was not so." See how he restores us to the ancient state.

Let me repeat what I said. But I ask you to help us in the struggle by keeping silent, so that no noise blows against us and scatters the thought. My Savior wanted to show that the teaching of the gospel leads us back to the original state. When the disciples, or rather the Pharisees, said, "Why did Moses command, 'If anyone divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce'?", the Savior did not accuse the law. Instead he spoke in its defense: "Moses said this because of your hardness of heart; but from the beginning it was not so." See how he restores us to the original state: "But he who made man made them male and female. What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate." In many places I find the Savior leading the good order of the church back to the original state. So the type of the church was lived out before circumcision. Now pay close attention. From the beginning the type of the church was lived out, and afterwards the rule of the church was lived out again, while the law came in between. The apostle wanted to show that the good order of the church runs in sequence through time, while the law only peeped in [?]. So he says, "But the law came in alongside." He did not say, "The law came in," but "came in alongside." For the law that came in is one thing, and the law that slipped in alongside is another. The gospel law came in from the beginning. It did not observe days, it knew no distinctions of foods, and it did not accept circumcision. This law was lived out from the beginning by the ancients, and it has come down to the last generations. In the middle the other law came in, or rather slipped in alongside. And one can hear the apostle say it plainly, as we have said: "The law came in alongside." Do you want to learn where it slipped in? Listen to the history. Jacob served Laban for Rachel, but at the wedding itself she did not come in [?]. The patriarch's aim was to take Rachel, but his father-in-law's deceit brought in one woman in place of another, and the one he had not sought was found to have been slipped in. In the same way God's aim was always to establish the church, but he brought in the synagogue alongside. He did not receive her by force and deceit; he was fitting events to the type of the ancient history. Jacob, while he was with Leah, kept his aim fixed on Rachel, though he bore the constraint that came from the deceit. So too God, during the time he had the synagogue, hated the one and longed for the other. What word bears witness to this for us? Who guarantees this reading of the history? Often God, while living with the synagogue under the law, said, "My soul hates your feasts and your new moons." Jacob loved Rachel's face but turned away from the weakness of Leah's eyes. "For Leah," it says, "was weak in the eyes." In the same way God turned away from the synagogue, not because she was unsound in body, but because she was blinded in soul. That is why the prophet said, "Who is blind but my servants? And who is deaf but those who rule them? And the servants of God were blinded." There he turned away because of weak eyes; here he turned away from the synagogue because of a blinded soul. That is why the Savior hinted at their blindness when he said, "Let them alone; they are guides of the blind. And if a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit." Throughout the whole time in which the synagogue lived under the law, God wanted to cast that people out because of their ingratitude. A prophet testifies to this somewhere, saying, "From the day I brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt until this day, it was before my eyes to cast out this city." And again, all the while the synagogue was joined to the law, God kept his aim on the church. So he says to Moses, "Let me alone, and I will make you into a great nation, and much more." If you hold this, that the church is the image of the ancient history [?], how did the law slip in alongside? As Leah did alongside Rachel. Brothers, this is not speculation or forced allegory. This story of Jacob truly was an image, and Jacob fulfilled the type of God, who once had the synagogue and now has the church. God himself cries out through the prophet: "I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented. And Jacob served for a wife, and for a wife he kept guard over me." Why then did he keep guard, or how did he keep guard? By another line of interpretation, brother, you will find that Jacob took his wife in one way and Isaac, Jacob's father, in another. When Isaac took his wife, he did not go to Mesopotamia himself to take her. He sent his servant and betrothed her through him. Jacob, however, did not betroth through a servant but in person. This too was a type of the old and the new. For God betrothed the old synagogue through his servant Moses and took her. Isaac, taking a wife, betroths through a servant, and having betrothed through a servant, he takes her. Jacob does not send a servant, though he had servants; he came to Mesopotamia himself. He came alone, though he had many servants. He came alone, though he had many beasts of burden. For God had blessed the house of his master Abraham with cattle and silver and gold and slaves and horses and everything else. With all these possessions, he comes with nothing but his staff. As Jacob says, "With my staff I crossed this Jordan," meaning: "With only a staff I went out alone, though I was master of much." Jacob went out alone. He came to Bethel, lay down to sleep in the evening, and put a stone under his head. He found no house and no lodging. For he was an image of the one who said, "But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Then, brothers, as he sleeps, he sees heaven opened. Christ had nowhere on earth to lay his head, but heaven and the things of heaven were opened to him. In the same way Jacob sleeps without a house, and he sees heaven opened and a ladder set up from earth to heaven. In another respect he was also a type of those who are persecuted. He came to Mesopotamia fleeing Esau, and God wanted to show that heaven is opened to everyone persecuted on earth. So Jacob sees heaven opened, and a ladder set up from earth to heaven, and the angels of God going up and coming down by the ladder. "And the Lord," it says, "was leaning upon it." It did not simply say that he sat, but that he leaned on the ladder. What is the ladder? An image of the cross. For it is through the cross that one can go up to heaven. Some went up to heaven through it, and others came down through it. The Jews fell from heaven through the cross, and the gentiles are led up to heaven through the cross.

But we must avoid forced allegory everywhere and seal what we say with the testimony of Scripture. The Savior shows through the Gospels that those angels going up and coming down fulfilled an image of the grace of the gospel. He says to Nathanael, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these. Truly I say to you, from now on you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God going up and coming down upon the Son of Man." Jacob came to Mesopotamia, and when he saw the vision, he said, "This is none other than the house of God." And yet you saw no houses being built, but a ladder. But since he knew that the ladder was a type of the church, he says, "This is the house of God; this is the church." How do we know that the house of God is the church? Paul says it, writing to Timothy: "If I am delayed, I write so that you may know how one ought to behave in the house of God, which is the church of the living God." Then, fulfilling the image of Christ in every way, owning nothing, hating wealth, and admitting no worldly illusion, Jacob says, "If the Lord God is with me and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear." See how the soul that loves wisdom does not go beyond what is sufficient. "If the Lord God is with me and guides me on the way and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear." Before the Gospels existed, he speaks the words of the apostles. "And if he gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear." Paul speaks through Jacob: "If we have food and covering, with these we shall be content." "This place shall be a house of God for me." For that is what Bethel means: "Beth" is "house," and "El" is "of God." He went to Mesopotamia, and the first thing he met was a well. He came to the well, and it was covered, and he found shepherds there. This is an image of Christ in every respect. Christ's first coming was to baptism, to the well, the well springing up to eternal life. The well is found covered, because grace too was veiled before his coming. Jacob says to the shepherds, "Why are you still standing here? It is still broad day. Water the sheep and take them away." They said to him, "Unless all the shepherds come, we cannot roll away the stone." And what does Jacob do at once? What had to be done by many, by all the shepherds, he does alone. He takes hold of the stone and rolls it away. How could he do alone what many could barely do? Because he was an image of Christ, and Scripture was showing the power of the Master: what many could not accomplish, the grace of the gospel accomplished. There he finds Rachel coming. Everywhere, for the most part, the righteous men of old received their brides at wells. Moses got his wife, the daughter of Jethro, at a well. Jacob found his at a well. Abraham's servant received Rebecca at a well. Everywhere the betrothals of the ancients come from a well, because Christ too betroths the church in no other way than from the waters. To be brief: he went in, he asked for Rachel, and Leah slipped in. We must keep to our subject, and we have to return to it. So the law slipped in alongside; it did not come in, just as Leah did not come in either, but slipped in. To come in is to act openly, with nothing hidden. To slip in is to come in sideways, together with someone else. So sin also slipped in; the devil slipped in through the law. "For sin, seizing the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me." So that no one may think the commandment is what deals death, he says, "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good. Did what is good, then, become death to me? By no means! It was so that sin might be shown up, working death in me through what is good." Everywhere he calls sin sinful, meaning the devil. "So that the devil," he says, "might be shown to be sinful beyond measure, working death through the commandment." "We know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal." You, Paul, carnal? You who are steered by the Holy Spirit, who have Christ speaking in you? If you are carnal, why did you deceive your disciples by saying, "You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit"? Your disciples are not in the flesh, and you are carnal? "But I am carnal." "I": who is that? The man who lived before the law and under the law. "Sold under sin." He did not say "sold by sin," but "sold to sin." No other person sold him; he sold himself. Among us humans, some are sold by force, while others who have their freedom hand themselves over into slavery by marrying slave girls or through some other necessity. In the same way man, who was free by nature and had been given a free nature, sold himself of his own will. Do you want to see a man selling himself? See what Elijah says to Ahab when God sent him to rebuke Ahab for the vineyard he had taken from Naboth. Ahab says to him, "Have you found me, my enemy?" Elijah says to him, "I have found you, because you sold yourself to do evil in the sight of the Lord." For we are sold through works of wickedness. "But I am carnal, sold under sin." For someone held captive by bad habit cannot easily throw himself out of slavery, even if he wants to. Habit is a second nature, and nature [prevails?] over human beings [?]. That is why he added, "For what I want, that I do not do," as one sold once and for all, "nor do I practise what I wish." These words suit a slave. Someone like that does not do what he wants but what he is ordered to do. In the same way man had no power to do what he wanted, only what sin ordered him to do. For from then on sin reigned, and no one could contradict a king. So man had been sold. This was not Paul, but an image of man, the creature made for freedom. To be brief: once he had said this, he added many proofs of forced slavery. "Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from the body of this death?" Do you see how he presented man as tested in bitter slavery and tyranny, longing to throw off his slavery, seeking freedom, and calling out for help? "Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me?" Who is coming? "I thank God through our Lord Jesus Christ." He wants to show you that by "sold to sin" he means the man who was once under the law, and by the freedom of those who were sold he means those redeemed through the grace of the gospel. So he says, "Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me? I thank God through our Lord Jesus Christ. He set me free from the law of sin. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus set me free." Do you see how he presented both the man being set free and the man in slavery? And he speaks not about himself alone, but about all humanity together. "For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus set me free from the law of sin and death." How were you set free? "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh." The law commanded what was good, but the flesh did not obey, because it was sold to sin. What the law could not accomplish because of the weakness of the flesh, he accomplished through the power of Christ's flesh. "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh" (for the law was not weak in itself, but through the flesh), "God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh: he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the just requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." So by the grace of God the questions have been answered. Paul does not say these things about himself. He does not slander his own freedom, nor place himself under sin, nor present himself as both spiritual and carnal. In his words he set up, as if in a picture, the man before the law [?], the man under the law, and the man after grace. Then he led us to recognize who man was before the law, who he was under the law, and who he is after the freedom that is in Christ. "God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh."

Here the other question is solved as well. Not only the Apollinarians but also the Arians and Eunomians say that the Savior assumed only flesh and not a soul too. Some of them, trying to seem generous, spoke of a soul without a mind; others said the Savior took flesh alone. But we showed in what we said yesterday that when Scripture mentions a human being, it is accustomed to name him by a part. Sometimes it names the whole human being from the flesh: "To you all flesh shall come," meaning every human being. Sometimes it names him from the soul, as when it says, "Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy-five souls." Sometimes it names him from the breath, as in, "Let every breath praise the Lord." Show me, then, where Scripture speaks of flesh without a soul. When it has died completely, it is no longer called flesh but a dead body. As long as it has the power of life and is alive, it is called flesh. Once it is dead, it is not called flesh but is termed a body. For everything without a soul is a body: a stone is a body, wood is a body, and a spirit [?] that has no soul is called a body. But tell me, why did he not assume the soul? "He came," they say, "to save by himself, and he had no need of our soul." Why then did he assume the flesh? "Since he could not appear as God, he assumed flesh, so that through it he might be believed." So the flesh had no soul? Then how did he hunger? How did he thirst? How did he grow weary? If you throw out the soul and bring in God in its place, you attribute hunger and thirst to him as well. Besides, brothers, suppose there were not both God the Word and an ensouled man, the vessel of humanity united to him, but only the Godhead in flesh. Then what soul was the Savior speaking of when he said, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit"? If there was only Godhead and no soul, who was it that committed, and what was committed? "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit," that is, my soul. If you posit only the Godhead in the flesh and throw out the soul, who commits, and what is committed? But the heretics' aim is clear. They say the Lord did not assume a soul so that they can drag all the lowly sayings onto the Godhead. When they read, "I do not speak on my own, for my Father has given me a commandment, what to say and what to speak," they want to ascribe it no longer to the humanity but to the Godhead. Do you see into what an abyss of impiety they slide? What is the spirit of which he says, "Into your hands I commit"? However much they strain, they cannot find it. The answer is found in other passages: he called the soul "spirit." Listen to Stephen saying at his martyrdom, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Stephen testifies that the spirit is the soul. Who, then, commits the spirit, and to whom [?] was the spirit committed? What substance is he talking about? The one to which the apostles apply the prophecy: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption." "You will not abandon my soul to Hades." Was this said about God? God is not left in Hades. Did Hades hold God? Did corruption hold the power that gives life? Did you not hear Paul say, "since it was not possible for the life to be held by corruption"? By "the life" he means the body. If the body is life, was life held by death? "You will not abandon my soul to Hades." The whole had fallen, and he raised the whole. The whole man had fallen, and he renewed the whole man. "But if you say," they object, "that he renewed a complete man, what difference do you allow between him and the apostles? For God was in them too." But to dwell in someone is one thing; to assume and be united is another. Of us it is said, "I will dwell in them and walk among them." He means the simplicity of the soul; he has in view the virtue of the soul, on which God rests and among which he walks. But the body of Christ himself, united from the womb, became a temple. It did not receive God to dwell in it through progress in its way of life. At the same moment the temple was built and God dwelt in it. So the body was the temple of the united Christ. That is why he says, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Oh, the absurdity of those who dare anything without fear! But enough said against the heretics who speak of soul and body and spirit and twist the apostle's saying: "God will keep your body and soul and spirit." This much must be said: they think the spirit is the mind. If the spirit is the mind, why does the apostle say, "I will sing with my spirit, and I will sing with my mind also"? If spirit and mind are the same thing, why does Paul divide them, saying, "I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also"? If the spirit is the mind, why does he speak of the mind as something other than the spirit? "But since," one says, "you did not accept it that way, explain it as you understand it." What does Paul mean when he says, "God will keep your body and soul and spirit"? Scripture is accustomed to call the gift of the Holy Spirit "spirit." I beg you, share my toil with me. For it is no small thing to cut out a heretical thorn. Scripture is accustomed to call the gift of the Holy Spirit "spirit." For example, if someone receives a spirit of wisdom or a spirit of knowledge, the gift of the Spirit itself is called spirit. Paul says, "Since you are eager for spirits," meaning for spiritual gifts. For there are not many Spirits. "Since you are eager for spirits, I will show you a still more excellent way." "I will show you," he means, "which of the gifts you ought to seek." So the grace of the Spirit is called spirit: not the very substance of the Spirit, but the working of the Spirit. "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit." The working of the Spirit is the spirit, that is, the gift, not the very substance of the Spirit. You are called spiritual, and the gift you have is called spirit. Is the apostle not saying, then, "God will keep your body and soul and the gift you received from the Spirit"? Again he calls the gift spirit. The gift grows through diligence and is lost through neglect. The apostle says, "Do not quench the Spirit." It is not possible to quench the substance of the Spirit, nor the mind, which exists by nature. But since we increase grace through diligence and quench it through laziness, he is saying, "Do not quench the gift you have received." So he calls the working of the Spirit "spirit." May we all attain it, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
